studies.title: God Is Enough As Trustee
studies.meaning: Four instructions open the surah, and their order matters. Be conscious of God; do not comply with those who reject and those who dissemble; follow what is revealed; rely on God. The middle instruction implies pressure was being applied, and the commentators read the sequence as describing what makes a person able to resist it. The closing clause is not encouragement but a sufficiency claim: one trustee is enough, so no second arrangement needs to be made alongside Him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the head of a surah that deals with a siege of the city and with the household of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Commentators describe a period of pressure from several directions at once, with proposals and compromises reaching him from opponents outside and from people inside the city whose commitment was uncertain. The instruction not to comply is read against that setting rather than against one named incident.

keyTerms.note: From a root for shielding and taking cover. The word describes an attentive wariness rather than fright, and it is the first thing asked for because everything after it depends on that attention.
The verb covers acting on someone's wish, not merely agreeing with it. What is forbidden here is the practical accommodation that begins long before anyone changes their mind.
The term for someone given power to act on another's behalf in his absence. It belongs to commerce and to the management of property, so the reliance described is a delegation rather than a feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina in these years was a city of arrangements. Clans held old alliances, some with groups outside the city, and every decision was weighed against who might be offended by it. A leader survived by managing that web, and the ordinary technique was accommodation: a concession here to hold a friendship there. These opening ayat address a man inside exactly that pressure and tell him the calculation runs differently.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of only a handful of surahs that open by addressing the Prophet directly with a vocative rather than by praising God, describing the Book or swearing an oath. The same opening form appears at the head of two other surahs, both also from the Medinan period, and each of the three then turns to a matter of the household or the community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Trust is defined here as an alternative to compliance rather than as a mood accompanying it. The word for trustee comes from the vocabulary of agency, so what is asked is the transfer of a matter into someone else's competence, which is why the passage can pair it with a flat refusal to accommodate anyone. Sufficiency is the load-bearing claim: enough removes the reason to keep a second option open.

crossReferences.why: Warns against the same accommodation, that they would like some softening in order to soften themselves.
Joins consultation with reliance, showing that trust does not replace deliberation but follows it.
Repeats the instruction to rely on the Living who does not die, in a Meccan setting.

studies.applyIt: Think of one small accommodation you make regularly to keep something smooth, a thing you go along with rather than agree with. Notice it once this week without changing anything. The passage puts the refusal to comply next to reliance on God for a reason, and you will usually find the accommodation is holding a fear in place.

studies.title: Two Hearts In One Body
studies.meaning: An image about anatomy opens the ayah and is then turned against a way of speaking. Nobody carries two hearts in one chest, and on the same logic a form of words cannot turn a wife into a mother or an adopted son into a son. Two customary declarations of that society are named and set aside as speech rather than fact. The closing contrast is between what mouths produce and what God says, so the whole ayah is about the limits of naming.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Two established practices are in view. In one, a man declared his wife to be to him like his mother, a formula that broke the marriage in effect while leaving her bound to him. In the other, a man adopted a boy, gave him his own name, and the boy was treated as a son in inheritance and in household relations. The commentators describe both as ordinary customs, and the ayah addresses the customs rather than any individual.

keyTerms.note: A dual form. The heart in this vocabulary is the seat of resolve and loyalty, so the image is not anatomical. It denies that two full commitments can occupy the same place at once.
A verb built on the word for a back, taken from the exact wording of the old formula. Naming the practice by its own phrase keeps the ayah describing a custom rather than an emotion.
A plural from the verb to call. The term itself means those whom you call sons, so the vocabulary already contains the ayah's point: the relation resides in the calling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming did real work in that society. An adopted boy took his new father's name, inherited from him, and stood inside the household as blood kin did for the purposes of marriage and protection. A man's word could reorganise a family, and everyone accepted the result without further ceremony. A claim that speech does not alter what a thing actually is therefore cut against a legal habit as much as a social one.
studies.didYouKnow: Both customs named here are taken up again elsewhere rather than left at this ayah. The declaration that likens a wife to a mother opens a short Medinan surah, which begins by reporting a woman who disputed about it and records that her complaint was heard. The matter of adopted sons returns near the middle of this surah, in a single clause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A line is drawn between what language can arrange and what it cannot. Many social facts really are made by declaration, and the ayah says that some things are not social facts. It also sets human and divine speech in one sentence and distinguishes them by truthfulness rather than by power, which prepares the surah's later interest in the gap between what is said about people and what is the case.

crossReferences.why: Takes up the same declaration about a wife, reporting a dispute over it and the answer given.
States in one clause what this ayah implies about the Prophet and the men around him.
Addresses the harm names do when a label is fixed on someone by other mouths.

studies.applyIt: Think of one label you use about yourself that began as somebody else's description, a family verdict on what you are like, a word from school that stuck. This ayah says a name applied by a mouth does not settle what a thing is. Set that word down for a day and notice how much of it was ever yours to carry.

studies.title: Call Them After Their Fathers
studies.meaning: One clause carries the change: name them by their fathers, since that is more equitable in God's sight. Then two provisions immediately soften its edges. Where a father is not known, the relation is named another way, as brotherhood in faith and as a bond of association, so that nobody is left standing outside a description. And error is set aside, with responsibility attached only to what a heart deliberately intended. The correction and its cushioning arrive in the same breath.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the statement that speech does not make an adopted son a son. Commentators report that men adopted in the earlier period were known by the names of the households that had taken them in, so the change touched people by name inside a small city. The two provisions are read as addressing precisely that disruption: parentage nobody could supply, and long habit that would not break at once.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root for fair apportionment, the same root behind the word for an accurate balance. It says the alternative is fairer, rather than condemning what had been done before.
A word that covers both a patron and the person attached to him, since the tie names the bond rather than the direction. It supplies belonging where descent cannot be named.

A verb of aiming at something on purpose, built on the word for a supporting post. It puts the measure of accountability at intention, so a tongue running on habit is treated differently from a planned deception.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society organised by descent, a name was an address. It told others who would answer for you, who would avenge you, whose feuds you inherited and whose property you might one day hold. Changing what a man was called moved him inside that system. The provisions in this ayah exist because the change carried real costs for people whose fathers could not be named at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact comparative used here, more equitable, appears again in the Quran at the close of its longest ayah, the one instructing that debts be written down. In both places it concerns accuracy of record rather than warmth of feeling, which is how the classical commentators read its use for names: what is being protected is information.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together. Truthfulness about origins is treated as a question of justice rather than of preference, because a name carries claims about who owes what to whom. And the attached provisions show that correcting a practice is not permitted to strand anyone: those without known fathers are given a relation at once, and the weight of past habit is lifted. Accountability rests on intention, not on the words themselves.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same comparative for equity, there about setting debts down in writing accurately.
States the principle this ayah applies, that speech does not make an adopted son a son.
Also makes the heart's intention the measure rather than what the tongue happened to produce.

studies.applyIt: Someone near you is regularly described by something that is not quite accurate, at work or in the family, and everyone has stopped hearing it. Say the accurate version once this week, quietly, without making a point of it. This ayah treats getting a description right as a matter of fairness rather than of tact, which is a different reason to bother.

studies.title: Closer Than Their Own Selves
studies.meaning: Three statements about closeness, each measured against a different rival claim. The Prophet is nearer to the believers than they are to themselves, which the commentators explain as a priority of his call over a person's own preference. His wives are described as mothers to the community, a standing of honour rather than of descent. And blood relatives are placed nearer to one another in what God has written than the ties of migration were, with good done to close associates left in place.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. When the emigrants reached the city they were paired with local families in a bond the commentators describe as carrying inheritance in the earliest period. This ayah is read as returning inheritance to kinship while leaving that bond intact as a relation of care. The description of the household belongs to the same passage and to the surah's wider concern with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and those around him.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from a root that joins closeness to guardianship. It measures priority of claim rather than depth of affection, which is why one word can serve for two very different nearnesses here.

The plural of mother, used of a standing rather than a descent. Commentators read it as establishing honour and restraint towards the household, and note that it does not carry the ordinary consequences of kinship.
A passive participle from the word for a written row. It presents the arrangement as already recorded rather than newly decided, which is how the ayah settles a matter that had been in flux.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pairing of arriving emigrants with households of the city was among the boldest things the young community had attempted. Men who came with nothing were attached to families who fed and housed them, and the tie was spoken of as brotherhood in earnest rather than as a courtesy. Several years on, with property accumulated and children born, the question of who inherited from whom had become live and awkward.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative that opens this ayah, meaning nearer or having the greater claim, is used twice inside it: once of the Prophet in relation to the believers, and once of blood relatives in relation to each other. One word does two different jobs in a single sentence, and the classical commentators treat the repetition as deliberate, marking two distinct kinds of nearness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah arranges claims rather than affections, and it does so in layers. Prophetic authority is set above a person's own inclination, which is a statement about where guidance comes from. Kinship is given back its precedence in what is recorded. The household is given a standing that is honorary rather than biological. Each layer is expressed in the language of writing, so none of it depends on how anyone feels.

crossReferences.why: States the same precedence of blood relatives in the Book of God, in nearly identical wording.
Makes the priority concrete, describing believers who call him to arbitrate and feel no resentment.
Lists the ties of family and property that can compete with God and His Messenger for loyalty.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this ayah settles who has a claim on you and says nothing about how you should feel about it. Pick one obligation you owe a relative that you have been carrying as a mood rather than a duty. Do the small version this week, the call or the visit, and let the feeling arrive afterwards or not at all.

studies.title: A Solemn Pledge From The Prophets
studies.meaning: A covenant taken from the prophets is recalled, and five of them are named. No content is given for the pledge, only its weight, which the commentators note is unusual and read alongside passages elsewhere that describe prophets undertaking to deliver and to confirm one another. The second ayah then supplies the purpose, and it is not what a reader expects: the truthful will be asked about their truthfulness. A covenant is turned into something that will later be examined.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed between the arrangement of household and kinship and the account of a siege. The passage grounds the instruction at the surah's opening, to follow what is revealed and not to accommodate anyone, in a commitment much older than the present moment. Commentators report no particular occasion for these two ayat and read them as supplying the frame within which the rest of the surah's demands are made.

keyTerms.note: From a root for binding tight, the same root behind a fastened knot and a trusted thing. It names an agreement made secure rather than merely stated, which is why the following word can intensify it further.
An adjective of physical thickness applied to an agreement, so the image is of something heavy in the hand. The same pairing of words is used elsewhere in the Quran of the bond of marriage.
The participle from a root covering truth in speech and steadiness in conduct together. That this group is the one questioned about its own truthfulness is the whole force of the second ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements in that world were secured by ceremony rather than by signature. Hands were struck together, oaths were sworn at a sanctuary, sometimes a garment was held while the words were spoken, and witnesses carried the exact wording in memory for years. The heaviest agreements were those made publicly before the most people. Calling a covenant thick placed it at the top of a scale everyone listening could rank.
studies.didYouKnow: These same five prophets appear as a group in only one other place in the Quran, where they are described as having been given one ordained religion. The membership of the two lists is identical. The order differs slightly: here the one addressed is named first among the five, while in the other passage he comes second, after Noah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is presented as a chain of commitments rather than a series of separate errands, and the covenant is described as taken rather than offered. The second ayah then makes truthfulness itself the object of questioning, which stops the covenant from working as a guarantee. Even those who kept it are asked about their keeping, and that keeps the relation between God and the reliable an accountable one rather than a settled account.

crossReferences.why: Names the same five prophets and says one religion was ordained through all of them.
Describes a covenant taken from the prophets to support a messenger confirming what they held.
Applies the language of a pledge kept to believers who held their ground under pressure.

studies.applyIt: Notice who gets questioned in the second ayah. Not the deniers, who are dealt with in half a clause, but the truthful, about their truthfulness. Take one thing you are confident you do well and ask a single hard question about it today, the kind you would put to somebody else without hesitating.

studies.title: A Wind And Unseen Forces
studies.meaning: The community is told to remember, and what follows is not a battle narrative but an inventory of what was sent. Armies came, and against them went a wind and forces the believers could not see. The classical commentators read the unseen forces as angels, present without being visible and, on most readings, without engaging. Nothing the believers themselves did appears in the sentence, which is what allows the whole episode to be framed as a favour to be recalled.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, recalling the siege of the city by an alliance of tribes some years after the migration. A trench was cut across the one open approach, the besieging camps sat outside it for weeks, and cold weather and wind eventually broke up their encampment, after which they withdrew. Commentators generally place the siege in the fifth year, though some reports give the fourth. This ayah opens the surah's account of it.

keyTerms.note: An imperative of deliberate recollection rather than of nostalgia. The community is asked to reconstruct a sequence on purpose, which is exactly what the ayat immediately following then do in detail.
The same word is used twice in the ayah, once of the besieging armies and once of what was sent against them. The repetition places both on one footing, differing only in visibility.
Indefinite in Arabic, so an unspecified wind rather than the wind. Commentators observe that the Quran mostly uses this singular of a destructive wind and the plural of winds bringing rain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trench was not an Arabian tactic. Raiding depended on speed and open ground, and a ditch across the approach removed the manoeuvre the attacking force was built around. Digging it occupied the whole city, in shifts, through cold weeks on short rations, and the work is remembered in reports for the songs sung over it. What this ayah asks the community to recall begins in that ground.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah takes its name from the word for the allied clans, which occurs twice inside it. Everywhere else in the Quran that word names something different: factions that divided over an earlier scripture, or the allied peoples of the distant past who opposed messengers before this time. Only in this surah does it name one particular coalition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is described as arriving in two forms, one ordinary and one entirely unseen, and the same noun is given to both. Weather and angels stand in a single list. That refuses the division between natural cause and divine action which most readers bring to such a passage, and it also declines to make the community's own effort the subject of the sentence, though that effort was real and is recorded elsewhere.

crossReferences.why: Describes angels sent in support at an earlier engagement, promised in similar terms.
Speaks again of forces that were not seen, sent down after a moment of hard pressure.
Answers a plea for help with a promise of angels, and calls the support reassurance rather than force.

studies.applyIt: Think back over one hard month you got through and list what actually helped, including the things you had no hand in arranging. Weather, timing, a person who happened to call that week. This ayah puts the unarranged help first. Write down three items and notice how many of them you have quietly been giving yourself credit for.

studies.title: When Hearts Reached The Throats
studies.meaning: The ayah is built out of physical detail. They came from above and from below, eyes swerved, hearts arrived at the throat. Then a clause that is remarkable for what it admits: you thought about God every kind of thought. The commentators do not soften it. They read the plural as covering the whole range present in the city that season, from steady confidence to something near despair, and they note that the ayah records the range rather than condemning it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the days of the siege from inside the city. Forces had taken position on the higher ground and on the lower approach, so the two directions in the ayah are topographical before they are rhetorical. Commentators describe cold, shortage of food, and word arriving that an arrangement protecting one flank had come apart. The ayah is read as an account of the worst stretch of those weeks.

keyTerms.note: A verb for deviation from a straight line, used elsewhere in the Quran of hearts turning aside. Applied to eyes it names a gaze that cannot settle, the particular look of someone unable to fix on anything.
An anatomical plural rather than a figure of speech in origin. The phrase compresses the whole sensation of terror into one location, and it has served as an idiom in Arabic ever since.
A definite plural of a word covering both supposition and suspicion. The article with the plural makes it every kind of thought at once, which is why the commentators decline to narrow its reference.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was not a walled city. It was a scatter of settlements, palm gardens and fortified stone houses across a plain, closed by lava fields on two sides with one open approach. Households sheltered in the strongholds while the men held the trench. The elevation this ayah describes was literal: attackers on the high ground could see down into the groves where families were waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word of this ayah is written with a final letter that is not sounded when the recitation runs on into the next. Setting aside the first-person pronoun, which is always spelled that way, only a few words in the whole text carry this feature, and three of them are in this surah: this one, and two more near its close. No other surah holds as many.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The community's doubt is put into the record. The believers are not described as unshaken, and nothing that follows treats their fear as disqualifying. That establishes something about how faith is measured here: not by the absence of the reactions this ayah lists, which are involuntary, but by what a person does while having them. The candour of the account is part of what it teaches.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether they expected the Garden without the shaking that earlier communities went through.
Uses the same image of hearts at the throats, there of the Day of Judgement.
Records a similar range of thoughts about God after a hard day, and names them plainly.

studies.applyIt: The next time fear arrives in your body before it reaches your thinking, notice that this ayah names the physical part first and does not treat it as a failure. Give it thirty seconds without arguing with yourself about it. What the passage measures is what you do in the following hour, not what your chest did in the first minute.

studies.title: There The Believers Were Tested
studies.meaning: One short ayah names what the previous description amounted to, and it uses two words: they were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking. The verb and its own noun are placed together, which in Arabic intensifies rather than repeats. Then the second ayah gives one thing that was said out loud during it, that the promise had been an illusion. The test is defined by the sentence it produced, not by the conditions that caused it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the account of the siege. The commentators explain that the speech quoted belongs to people within the city whose commitment had always been conditional, and to others described as having a sickness in the heart, a phrase the tradition reads as covering wavering rather than a settled position. No individual is named in the passage, and the commentators generally follow the Quran in leaving it that way.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the root for trying something to find out what it is, used of assaying metal. The passive matters: nobody in the ayah chose the test, and its purpose is disclosure rather than punishment.
The noun placed after its own verb to intensify it, a construction the Quran reserves for extremes. The same root names the earthquake that titles one of the short surahs near the end of the Book.
From a root for deceiving by appearance, the word used elsewhere for the deceptive attraction of worldly life. It accuses the promise of looking better than it was rather than of being untrue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A siege exposes a settlement's internal arithmetic. Every household in the city had relatives, trading partners or old alliances among the tribes camped outside, and everyone knew roughly who those were. Under pressure, people recalculate what they can survive, and the calculation is done quietly. The speech quoted in the second ayah is the sound of that arithmetic surfacing at the moment it seemed safe to say aloud.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing a sickness in the heart occurs about a dozen times in the Quran, spread across several Medinan surahs, and it is never attached to a name. The classical commentators discuss who was meant and record differing reports, but the text itself keeps the category open, which is how it stays legible to later readers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Testing is described in the passive and given a purpose that is neither punishment nor improvement but disclosure. What the shaking produced was speech, and the speech is what the Quran preserves. That suggests the point of a trial in this account is to make visible a position a person already held, which is why the same conditions produce two entirely different sentences from two groups standing in the same trench.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of shaking for earlier communities, with the messenger asking when help comes.
States the principle directly, that people are not left untested simply for saying they believe.
Says those with sickness in their hearts would be recognised by the drift of their speech.

studies.applyIt: Notice that what this passage records from the hardest week is not what anyone felt but what somebody said. Pick one pressured moment this week and pay attention to the sentence that comes out of you. You do not have to correct it. Just hear it accurately, since it is a better report on where you stand than your mood is.

studies.title: Our Homes Are Exposed
studies.meaning: Two withdrawals are described, and they are different in kind. One group calls out openly that there is no holding this position and tells people to go back. Another asks permission to leave, giving a reason: our houses are undefended. The ayah then does something unusual. It states flatly that the houses were not undefended, and names what the request actually was. An excuse is quoted, corrected, and translated in the space of one sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, during the siege of the city. The commentators explain that families were sheltering in fortified houses across the settlement while the men held the trench, so a claim that a house lay open was a claim about relatives at risk, which is the most difficult kind of request to refuse. The address uses the city's older name, which the commentators note was still in ordinary use at the time.

keyTerms.note: The settlement's older name, used here in an address by people distancing themselves from it. It appears only once in the Quran, and everywhere else the place is called simply the city.
The word for a breach in a defence, a place where something is uncovered and vulnerable. It is a military term here before it is anything else, describing a wall with a way through it.
The plain noun for running away, which the ayah supplies after quoting a more presentable reason. Setting the two words next to each other is the whole rhetorical move of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Withdrawing from a fight was not automatically shameful in that society if a reason could be produced. Obligations to protect one's own household were recognised and could outrank a wider commitment, and every man knew the accepted forms for invoking them. What the ayah addresses is not cowardice, which was despised openly, but the use of a legitimate category to cover something else. The vocabulary of duty was available to anyone.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the city is called Yathrib. Everywhere else it appears as the city, and the classical commentators note the older name is used here in the mouths of people separating themselves from the community. The word survives in inscriptions and in pre-Islamic poetry, which is how its antiquity is known.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a stated reason and a real reason as two different objects and shows that God's account of an action includes both. That is a claim about how deeds are assessed. It also implies that a good reason genuinely exists for the thing being invoked, since the ayah has to deny the facts rather than dismiss the category, which is precisely what makes such reasons usable in the first place.

crossReferences.why: Quotes a permissible-sounding request to be excused and names what lay behind it.
Records a true statement made by people whose speech the Quran nonetheless calls false.
Describes an easy journey they would have joined, and the oaths sworn to avoid a hard one.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you declined recently and the reason you gave. It was probably a true reason and not the whole reason. You do not need to go back and correct anyone. Just name the second half to yourself once, accurately. This ayah is interested in the gap between the two, and so, usually, is the person who was refused.

studies.title: The Pledge Not To Turn Back
studies.meaning: A hypothetical is put first: if the city had actually been entered from its edges and they had then been asked to change sides, they would have done it with barely a pause. The commentators read this as measuring a disposition rather than predicting an event. The second ayah supplies the fact that makes the hypothetical damning. These people had already given an undertaking not to turn their backs. The closing clause states plainly that an undertaking given to God is one that gets asked about.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the account of the siege. The commentators connect the earlier undertaking either to a general pledge given by the community or to a specific occasion when some had committed themselves after an earlier engagement, and they report the difference rather than settling it. What the passage assumes is that a public commitment had been made and was remembered by everyone, including those who made it.

keyTerms.note: A word whose root is the assaying of gold by fire. It covers a trial, a temptation and the act of turning someone from allegiance, and commentators read this occurrence in the last of those senses.
A verb for tarrying in a place. Its use with a word meaning a little compresses the whole judgement into a measure of time: not whether they would turn, but how long it would take.

A passive participle from the verb to ask. The undertaking itself is described as the thing that will be questioned, so the ayah makes the promise, rather than the promiser, the subject of the reckoning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Changing allegiance was an ordinary instrument of Arabian politics. Alliances shifted with advantage, and a clan that moved to the winning side at the right moment was often thought shrewd rather than treacherous. What made a commitment binding was the ceremony around it and the number of people who had witnessed it. This passage treats a pledge as binding for a different reason, and names the party who will ask about it.
studies.didYouKnow: The passive participle used at the end, meaning something that will be asked about, appears only a handful of times in the Quran and is applied elsewhere to a covenant in exactly the same way. In another passage the same form is used of the hearing, the sight and the heart, each said to be answerable in its own right.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas are set together. The first is that a disposition can be assessed on a situation that never arrived, which locates moral reality in a person's readiness rather than only in their record. The second is that a promise made to God carries a permanence that a promise between people does not, since the party who holds it does not forget, move away, or lose interest in collecting.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for a covenant, saying that an undertaking will be asked about.
Applies the same form to hearing, sight and heart, each answerable for what it did.
Describes a pledge given to the Messenger as a pledge given to God directly.

studies.applyIt: Think of one promise you made out loud and have quietly downgraded, to a child, a friend, yourself. Not broken, just softened. This passage says a commitment is a thing that gets asked about later. Say the promise back to yourself in its original wording today, without adjusting it, and see whether you still mean it.

studies.title: Who Will Shield You From God
studies.meaning: Two answers are given, both introduced by the instruction to say. The first is arithmetical: flight buys nothing, because even a successful escape from death only converts into a short remainder of enjoyment. The second is a question with no available answer, asking who could screen a person from God. What makes the second unusual is its symmetry. It names adversity and mercy together, so the point is not that nobody can protect you but that nothing gets between you and either outcome.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to those who had asked to withdraw from the defence of the city during the siege. Commentators read these two ayat as the answer to the request quoted a few lines earlier, and note that the reply argues rather than orders. What is offered is a reason to reconsider, framed in terms of what flight can and cannot actually secure.

keyTerms.note: A verb of gripping something to keep it from falling, used of a handhold and of restraint. It pictures protection as physical interception, which is why the question expects no answer.
A passive from the root for provision one benefits from temporarily. The passive removes the escaper's agency: even the reprieve he ran for turns out to be something handed to him.
One who comes to aid someone already in difficulty, distinct from the ally in the preceding word who is attached beforehand. The pair covers both kinds of backing a person might look for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection was the organising fact of Arabian life. A man travelled under the guarantee of a clan or a patron, and to be outside such a guarantee was to be legally exposed anywhere beyond your own valley. Guarantees could be bought, inherited or requested, and everyone knew whose name to invoke where. The question in the second ayah asks for a name in a system where a name had always been available.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah pairs adversity and mercy inside a single question, which is unusual. Most passages of this kind ask only who could avert a harm. Including mercy in the same sentence extends the point in both directions at once, and the classical commentators note the symmetry: nothing intervenes between a person and either of the two things God intends for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reframes safety as a question of duration rather than of escape. Nobody is told that they will not die; they are told that fleeing changes only how much time remains, which is a smaller claim and a harder one to argue with. Naming mercy alongside adversity then turns the whole argument around, so that the same absence of intermediaries which threatens also guarantees.

crossReferences.why: Says death will reach you even in fortified towers, addressed to a similar reluctance.
Answers those who thought staying home would have saved them, on the same reasoning.
Asks whether anything invoked besides God could remove a harm or hold back a mercy.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the second question here includes mercy as well as harm. Most of us only ever ask the first half. Take one good thing you are hoping for and consider that no arrangement of yours is holding it up, and none is holding it back either. Sit with that for a minute before you next try to arrange something.

studies.title: God Already Knows The Hinderers
studies.meaning: The ayah opens with a particle of confirmation and the verb to know, so the force is that this is already established and not newly discovered. Two groups are named by what they do rather than by who they are: those who hold others back, and those who invite their own people to come away and join them. The closing clause is a measurement. They turn up for hardship rarely, which the commentators read as an observation about pattern rather than a single absence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, during the siege of the city. The commentators describe quiet recruitment going on inside the settlement, with individuals working on their relatives rather than announcing a position publicly. No names are given in the Quran and the classical sources record differing reports about who was meant. The ayah addresses the behaviour, which is why it remains legible long after the particular people are gone.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a verb meaning to slow something down or make it late. It names people who obstruct by dragging rather than by refusing, which is a harder thing to point at.
An informal call used to summon someone near, closer to a beckoning than a command. Quoting it exactly reproduces the intimacy of the invitation, which was addressed to brothers and neighbours.
A word that covers force, harm and severe difficulty together, so it names the hard part of a situation rather than the situation itself. The ayah says these people show up for it seldom.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Persuasion in a city like Medina travelled through households, not assemblies. A man spoke to his brother in a courtyard, an uncle raised a doubt over food, and by the following week a whole family had shifted without anyone making a speech. That was the ordinary machinery of opinion in a settlement of a few thousand people. The ayah describes exactly that machinery being used, in its own vocabulary.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for hindering others appears only here in the whole Quran, in this single participle. The classical commentators explain it from the ordinary Arabic verb for delaying a thing, and its rarity is part of why they discuss the shade of meaning so carefully: the text provides no second occurrence to compare it against.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates knowledge of a private activity with God before any human authority has identified it, which changes what secrecy means. It also identifies a specific kind of harm, the discouragement worked on someone else, and treats it as a matter for reckoning in its own right. What is described is not opposition but drag, and the passage takes drag as seriously as refusal.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who lag behind and congratulate themselves when others meet difficulty.
Says some among them would have sown discord and moved about spreading unrest.
Quotes those invited to fight or to contribute, who answered that they did not know how.

studies.applyIt: Discouragement usually arrives as realism from someone who cares about you. Notice one place where you play that role for another person: the sentence you add that takes the air out of their plan. You do not have to become an enthusiast. Just leave the sentence unsaid once this week and see what they do with the space.

studies.title: Sharp Tongues When Fear Passes
studies.meaning: One word for withholding frames the whole ayah, appearing at the beginning and again near the end with different objects. Between them sits a portrait in two states. Under threat the eyes roll and the person is compared to someone losing consciousness at the point of death. Once the danger lifts, the same person is fluent and cutting. The commentators read the pairing as the argument: the fluency and the paralysis are the same condition showing two faces.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the siege of the city. The commentators explain that once the besieging force withdrew there were claims to be made about who had contributed and what was owed, and the ayah describes people pressing those claims loudly. The description is of behaviour during and immediately after the weeks of pressure rather than of any single meeting or occasion.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective from a root joining stinginess to eagerness, so it names greed with appetite in it rather than mere reluctance. The ayah uses it twice, first of their conduct and then of good itself.
A verb for scalding with heat and for striking with something hot, transferred to speech. It is a rare and physical word, and it gives the tongues in the same clause their edge.
The adjective used of a blade, from the root that also gives the word for iron. Applying it to tongues makes the comparison with a weapon exact rather than decorative.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a raiding economy, what a man had risked determined what he could claim afterwards. Distribution was argued out in the open, and reputation was made in that argument as much as in the fighting. A man who had been absent from the danger but eloquent in the settlement could still come away with standing. This ayah describes people working that gap, and its listeners would have recognised the type immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered here as lashing with the tongue occurs only once in the Quran. Its ordinary meaning is to scald or to strike with something heated, and the classical commentators explain it from that physical sense rather than from any established figurative usage, which suggests the image was still fresh when the ayah was recited.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Withholding is presented as a single disposition with several outlets, so meanness with effort, with money and with good will towards others are treated as one thing rather than three. The ayah then makes an unexpected move: it says these have not believed, and their works are void. Conduct under pressure is treated as evidence about a state rather than as an offence added to a record.

crossReferences.why: Names withholding as the point where a person is actually tested, and what it costs.
Describes those who wait to see the outcome and then present themselves to the winning side.
Shows the same sharp speech directed at those who gave what little they had.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you speak in the hour after a scare passes. Most people are ungenerous exactly then, and it comes out as sharpness towards whoever is nearest. Next time the pressure lifts, wait ten minutes before saying anything about how it was handled. That gap is where this ayah locates the difference between two kinds of person.

studies.title: Wishing They Were Among Bedouins
studies.meaning: The ayah describes a state of mind after the danger has passed rather than during it. They cannot believe the allied force has really gone, and if it returned they would want to be out in the desert with the nomads, sending in for news. The commentators note the precision of that wish: not simply to be absent, but to be somewhere safe while still following the story. The last clause adds that even present, they contributed little.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's account of the siege. The besieging alliance had withdrawn after weeks outside the trench, and the city was absorbing what had happened. Commentators read this ayah as describing people who remained inside the community afterwards without having been part of what it went through, which is why the surah spends several ayat on them rather than dismissing them in one.

keyTerms.note: A plural for parties or factions bound into a coalition. The surah takes its name from this word, and it names the alliance from outside rather than by any tribe's own name.
A participle for those living out in the desert rather than in a settlement. It carries no insult; it simply describes a way of life that keeps a person at a distance from a city's obligations.
A plural for reports of consequence rather than idle talk, the same root used of the accounts of earlier peoples. The wish is to receive the outcome as a report instead of living it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The relation between settled towns and the nomadic tribes around them was constant and practical. Townspeople had cousins in the tents; children were sometimes sent out to be raised there; herds moved between the two. Withdrawing into the desert during a conflict was a real option, and it did not require leaving your family behind. What the ayah describes is a plausible plan rather than an idle daydream.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of only two ayat in the surah that carry the word for the allied clans, and the surah is named after it. Elsewhere in the Quran the same word does not describe an army at all: it names factions that split over an earlier scripture, or the allied peoples of the distant past who opposed earlier messengers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belonging is measured here by exposure rather than by presence. These people are inside the community and physically inside the city, and the ayah still describes them as elsewhere, because their imagination is positioned at a safe distance and receiving reports. That makes membership a matter of what a person has actually risked, which is a harder standard than agreement and a more forgiving one than achievement.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who stayed behind while others went, and what such staying costs.
Quotes the excuse of those who remained with their property and families instead.
Gives the opposite reaction to the same allied force, seen by those who had been promised it.

studies.applyIt: There is probably one thing in your life you have arranged to follow rather than to be part of, near enough for the news and far enough for safety. A family situation, a difficulty at work. Move one step closer this week. Not the whole way. Just close enough that the news reaches you as something happening to you.

studies.title: An Excellent Pattern To Follow
studies.meaning: The word rendered as example means a model that is copied, and the sentence attaches a condition to it. It is an excellent pattern for whoever hopes for God and the last day and remembers God often, so what a person is looking for determines whether the pattern is available to them at all. The second ayah then shows the thing in operation. Facing an army assembled to finish them, the believers identified it as what they had been told to expect, and the recognition raised their confidence rather than lowering it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the siege in which allied clans marched on Medina. A ditch was dug across the exposed northern approach and held for weeks in cold weather with rations short and families moved into fortified quarters. The surah gives its opening section to that episode, and these two ayat sit deliberately between a description of those who found reasons to withdraw and a description of those who kept their word.

keyTerms.note: Something one takes as a template for one's own conduct, from a root connected with setting a thing right by matching it to another. It implies imitation in practice, not admiration at a distance.
The plural of a party or faction bound together for a purpose. It names an alliance of clans that would ordinarily be rivals, which is what made the sight of them outside the town so alarming.
From the root of peace and of handing something over intact. Paired with faith, it names the settling of the matter rather than the belief itself, the point where argument stops.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian warfare was raiding: a fast approach, a fight, a withdrawal within a day. A coalition camped outside a town for weeks was outside everyone's experience, which is part of why the ditch was dug at all. Men worked in shifts turning earth in the cold with rations short enough that the accounts remember what people did and did not eat during it.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah takes its name from that coalition, and the campaign carries two names in the tradition: one after the confederated clans who came, and one after the ditch that was dug against them. The same weeks are therefore remembered both by who arrived and by what was built, depending on which account is being told.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting a person rather than a rule as the model changes what following means. A rule can be satisfied exactly and then set down; a pattern has to be read into circumstances it never met, which requires the attention the same ayah calls frequent remembrance. The second ayah adds something about belief itself: it grew at the moment the danger was confirmed, so what strengthened them was accuracy rather than reassurance.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical word of Abraham and those with him, showing the pattern is not unique to one messenger.
States what is being copied in one line, that he stands upon a great and settled character.
Gives the narrative of the same siege, including the wind and the hosts that were sent against it.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose steadiness under pressure you have actually watched, not read about. Identify a single small thing they do, the pause before answering, the way they eat properly on a bad day, and copy that one thing this week. A pattern is only followed in details; admiring the whole of it costs nothing and changes nothing.

studies.title: Men True To Their Pledge
studies.meaning: A short ayah about keeping a word. The men described made an undertaking to God and matched it, and they are then sorted into two groups: those who have completed what they took on and those still waiting to. Scholars differ over the word for what was completed, reading it as a vow discharged, as a life run to its term, or as death met in the manner promised, and the commentaries record the range rather than settling it. The last clause states the whole matter negatively: they changed nothing at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the weeks of the siege of Medina. The classical sources connect the ayah with men who had given an undertaking before an earlier engagement and then held to it, and their reports name several individuals and differ over which is meant. What the accounts agree on is the shape of the situation: a pledge given while nothing was happening, and kept once the danger arrived and the reasons for withdrawing had become obvious.

keyTerms.note: A mutual undertaking, from a root meaning to keep something in view and return to it. The word implies an obligation a person is expected to revisit rather than one discharged and forgotten.
A word that occurs only here in the whole Quran, which is why the commentaries record several readings of it: a vow paid, a lifespan completed, or a death accepted in advance.
To put one thing in the place of another. Denying it twice over, with a noun repeating the verb, is a construction of emphasis: not the smallest substitution was made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in Arabia was public and physical, given by clasping hands in front of witnesses, and it bound a man's whole standing. Someone who broke one was satirised in verse and the verse outlived him. In fighting, a man who had sworn to hold a position and then left it was disgraced permanently, and the memory of it attached to his sons, so the cost of a broken pledge was measured in generations.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated as vow in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. A single occurrence gives the philologists very little to work from, which is exactly why the classical commentaries preserve three readings of it side by side rather than choosing, and why translations of this line differ from one another more than usual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is presented as a match between a sentence and a later life rather than as accuracy in reporting facts. The division into those who have finished and those still waiting is the striking part: the ones who have not yet been tested are counted among the truthful already, so the category is defined by an intention that has not moved rather than by an outcome that can be checked.

crossReferences.why: Describes a pledge given by hand and states plainly what fulfilling it is answered with.
Includes keeping a covenant once made in its short list of what actually counts as righteousness.
Puts the same undertaking as a transaction and asks who is more faithful to a covenant than God.

studies.applyIt: Find one promise you made that has quietly gone unmentioned for months. This week either do it, or tell the person plainly that you will not and why. The ayah's final phrase is about not substituting anything, and a promise silently replaced by nothing is the substitution that is easiest to make and hardest to notice.

studies.title: Or He May Turn To Them
studies.meaning: A purpose clause gathers up everything the surah has described so far. The truthful are rewarded for their truthfulness, and then the second half breaks the symmetry a reader is braced for. Punishment is made conditional on God's will, and pardon is named as the alternative in the same breath, about the very people the preceding ayat have just exposed. The next ayah reports the outcome plainly: the besiegers went back in their rage, having gained nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's account of the siege. The allied force withdrew after weeks outside the trench, and the ayah describes the ending without a battle: the believers were spared the fighting. Commentators note that the passage names no engagement and gives the outcome to God rather than to the defence, which matches reports that the encampments broke up in bad weather rather than in combat.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used of a person repenting is used here of God, and its root means simply to turn. When God is its subject it names an acceptance offered before anyone has asked.
A word for anger that has been swallowed rather than released, the fury of someone who could not act on it. It describes the state they left in, not the state they arrived in.
A verb of being enough for a task, taking the believers as its object and the fighting as what they were spared. The construction credits the outcome to God without denying anyone's effort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A besieging force in that country was expensive. Allied tribes brought their own animals and supplies, and every week outside a settlement cost them grazing, trade and patience with each other. Coalitions of that size were held together by the expectation of a quick result. When weeks passed with nothing gained, the arithmetic that assembled the alliance began to work in reverse, and the camps thinned.
studies.didYouKnow: The first of these two ayat ends by naming God as Forgiving and Merciful, immediately after describing punishment. The pairing of those two names appears more often than any other pair of divine names in the Quran, and the classical commentators note that its usual position is at the close of a passage about failure, not at the close of a passage about reward.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are refused at once. Symmetry is refused, since reward is stated as settled while punishment is left conditional and pardon is held open. And the reader's satisfaction is refused: the group the surah has just described at length is not disposed of. Nothing in the wording rules out any of them turning, which leaves the question of who ends where genuinely open in a way readers rarely allow.

crossReferences.why: Also leaves open that God may turn towards a group He has just described as hostile.
Names the harshest position for the dissembling and then makes an exception for those who repent.
Sets out the opposite ending for the same category, so the two passages should be read together.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last person you decided was simply a certain kind of person. This ayah takes the group it has spent fifteen lines exposing and refuses to close their file. You do not have to change your assessment of anyone today. Just stop treating your assessment as the final version, and notice how much of your irritation was resting on it.

studies.title: Brought Down From Their Strongholds
studies.meaning: The ayah reports the aftermath of the siege in four clauses and does not soften any of them. A group described as having backed the besiegers was brought down from its fortified towers, dread was put into their hearts, some were killed and others taken. The word chosen for the towers occurs nowhere else in the Quran. What the sentence does not contain is any note of celebration, and the classical commentators read it as record rather than as commendation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the withdrawal of the allied force. The classical accounts describe a Jewish tribe of the city, bound to the community by treaty, which the sources report had come to an understanding with the besiegers during the weeks of the siege. After the withdrawal they held out in their strongholds and then surrendered, asking that the matter be settled by an arbitrator from a tribe long allied to them. His judgement fell as this ayah describes.

keyTerms.note: A rare plural for strongholds, from a root also used of the horn of an animal and the spur of a cock, meaning what a creature defends itself with. It occurs only here in the Quran.

A verb from the word for a back, meaning to stand behind someone in support. The same root appeared earlier in this surah for a very different declaration, which is a coincidence of vocabulary rather than of sense.
A fear that fills and empties a person rather than one that prompts flight. The Quran always describes it as cast or thrown into hearts, never as something a human party produces.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The settlements around the city were built for exactly this. A tribe's strength lay in its stone towers and walled gardens, stocked with dates and water against a siege that might last months. Holding out was the standard response to any pressure, and it usually worked, because attackers rarely had the supplies to wait. What the ayah records is the failure of the ordinary defence of that country.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the strongholds here appears only once in the whole Quran. Its root is used in Arabic for a horn and for the spur of a fighting bird, so the towers are named by the image of a creature's own weapon. The classical lexicographers gathered this usage from poetry rather than from any second scriptural occurrence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A difficult event is placed in the record without decoration on either side. Nothing here is presented as a triumph of the community, since every verb has God as its subject and the human role appears only in the last clause. That framing carries a cost the passage accepts: what happened is not made anyone's achievement, and it is not made to disappear either. The Quran keeps its own hardest history in view.

crossReferences.why: Describes another group leaving its strongholds, and says their own hands destroyed their houses.
Sets out how broken agreements were to be handled, including notice given before any action.
Uses the same word for dread cast into hearts, and attributes the casting to God alone.

studies.applyIt: This is a hard ayah and it is not made easier by hurrying past it. Read it once slowly and notice that the Quran does not congratulate anyone in it. When you next tell the story of something difficult that went your way, try telling it that flatly, without the part where you come out well. It is a discipline the text is modelling.

studies.title: A Land You Had Not Trodden
studies.meaning: Three concrete items are listed, land and houses and possessions, and then a fourth that does not belong to the same category: a land you have not set foot on. The classical commentators differ over what that fourth refers to. Some read it as a nearby settlement that came later, some as the wider territories that opened to the community afterwards, some as everything that would follow. They record the range without deciding. The ayah closes on power rather than on entitlement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the account of the siege and its aftermath. Property left by a departed or defeated group was distributed under arrangements the Quran sets out elsewhere in some detail, and the commentators discuss those arrangements rather than treating this ayah as the rule. What this ayah supplies is the framing: the transfer is described as something God caused, using the vocabulary of inheritance rather than of capture.

keyTerms.note: The causative of the verb to inherit, so the transfer is described as a bequest arranged by someone else rather than as a seizure. The Quran uses the same verb of nations succeeding nations on the earth.
A plural covering not just buildings but the whole settled area a group occupies, its quarter of a town. It is the same word used across the Quran for what people are driven out of.
The verb for setting a foot on ground. Its use makes the fourth item in the list purely future, defined by an absence of contact, which is why the commentators could not fix its reference.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land in and around the city was not open range. It was walled gardens, date palms counted individually, and irrigation channels whose shares were known to everyone. Wells were owned in fractions and inherited by name. To speak of receiving land, homes and property in that setting was to speak of an accounting exercise of great precision, not of a vague windfall, and every item had a former holder people could name.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the verb for causing someone to inherit of very different things: a defeated people's property here, the earth given to God's servants in another passage, and the Garden itself in several. The classical commentators note that the same word covers all three, so possession in the Quran's vocabulary is consistently something received rather than something taken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The framing does real work. By describing the transfer as an inheritance caused by God, the ayah denies that conquest establishes a right, since an inheritor holds what was assigned rather than what he won. The unvisited land then extends the point past anything the audience could have arranged. And the closing name is about power rather than about justice, which leaves the moral assessment to the passages that address it elsewhere.

crossReferences.why: Sets out how property gained without fighting was to be distributed, and to whom.
Uses the same verb of the righteous inheriting the earth, in a much wider frame.
Says an oppressed people were made to inherit the lands they had been kept from.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you own that you think of as earned. Trace back the parts of it you did not arrange: where you were born, who taught you, the year the market moved. This ayah calls property an inheritance even when it arrives at the end of a struggle. Sit with the word inheritance over one possession today and see what it changes.

studies.title: Let Me Release You Kindly
studies.meaning: An offer is put in the Prophet's mouth and he is told to make it aloud. If what you want is this life and its ornament, come and I will provide for you and let you go, well. Two things are notable. The choice is real, with provision attached to it rather than shame, and the word for the release is qualified as gracious, so no version of leaving is described as a disgrace. The commentators read the whole ayah as removing pressure rather than applying it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical accounts describe a period in which the household of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was living with very little while the community around it was becoming more prosperous, and reports describe a request for a wider share of that provision. The commentators connect this ayah and the one following to that setting, and describe the offer as having been put to each member of the household individually.

keyTerms.note: The word for what is added to a thing to make it attractive rather than the thing itself. Naming the ornament and not the life makes the choice about surplus, which is a narrower and fairer question.
A verb for giving something to be enjoyed for a period, used in the Quran of provision made at a parting. It ensures the offer carries material support rather than only permission to leave.
An adjective of beauty applied to the manner of a release. The Quran attaches it elsewhere to patience and to overlooking, always to describe doing a hard thing without bitterness in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household's standing was visible in ordinary things: how many changes of clothing, whether there was oil for the lamp, how often meat appeared. Women in that society had defined claims on maintenance, and those claims were discussed openly among families. A request for more was not extraordinary or shameful; it was the normal working of an arrangement everyone understood, which is what makes the answer here surprising.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a gracious release appears only twice in the Quran, both times in this surah. The second occurrence, some twenty ayat later, applies it in a general setting rather than a household one. In both places the adjective for beauty is attached to the parting itself, which is not how partings are usually described.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a genuine alternative in front of people close to a prophet, which says something about how such closeness works. It cannot be maintained by obligation or by embarrassment, and the offer of provision is what makes the choice honest rather than nominal. Renunciation is also defined narrowly here, as declining an ornament rather than as accepting hardship, which keeps the demand proportionate.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half of the same offer and what is prepared for those who stay.
Warns against straining the eyes towards the ornament of this life given to others.
Calls wealth and children the ornament of this life, then names what actually lasts.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this offer names the ornament rather than the life. Nobody is asked to want less of the thing itself, only of what has been added to it for show. Pick one item in your home that exists mainly to be seen. You do not have to remove it. Just identify it accurately today, and stop counting it as part of what you need.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: If You Desire God
studies.meaning: The second half of an offer, and the two halves are not built the same way. The first named a thing wanted and a provision to be given. This one names three objects of desire together, God, His Messenger and the final home, and then does not promise them. What is promised instead is something prepared, described only as immense. The commentators note that the reward is left undescribed on purpose, and that the condition attached is excellence in conduct rather than the desire itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the choice put to the household of the Prophet in the previous ayah. The classical accounts describe the offer being made individually and the answer given being the same in each case. The commentators read the pairing of the two ayat as the point: a genuine alternative had to be stated first for the answer to this one to mean anything at all.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb of wanting, repeated from the previous ayah with a completely different object. Using one word for both sides makes the choice a matter of direction rather than of intensity.
The ordinary word for a dwelling and its courtyard, the place a family belongs to. Applying it to what comes after death describes the hereafter as a residence rather than as a condition.

keyTerms.gloss: for the women who do well
keyTerms.note: From the verb for doing something beautifully. The reward attaches to conduct rather than to the desire named at the start, so wanting the right thing is where the ayah begins, not where it ends.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage in that society was among other things an economic arrangement, with agreed maintenance and a settlement due at its ending. A woman offered provision and a dignified release was being offered something real and enforceable. Turning it down meant accepting a household whose income was largely given away and whose door was open to petitioners all day. The choice had a price that everyone in the city could have calculated.
studies.didYouKnow: The three objects of desire in this ayah are named in ascending order, and the third is a place rather than a person or a state. The exact phrase for that final home occurs six times in the Quran, and in most of them it stands in open contrast with the nearer life. It is also the only one of the three a reader can picture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Desire is treated as the thing being tested, and desire is not a duty that can be imposed. That is why the previous ayah had to offer a real way out: an unforced answer is the only kind that means anything here. The reward is then left unspecified, which keeps it from becoming a second ornament, a better bargain offered against the first. What is being asked for is a direction of wanting.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first half of the offer and the provision attached to the other choice.
Describes those who call on their Lord wanting His face, and warns against looking past them.
Puts the same purity of motive in speech: we feed you only for God's face.

studies.applyIt: Try naming what you actually want this week, in one sentence, before naming what you should want. Most people never do the first, so the second has nothing to correct. This ayah begins by asking about desire rather than about behaviour, which is a more uncomfortable question and a more useful one to have answered honestly.

studies.title: Where A Fault Would Count Double
studies.meaning: A conditional is stated about the household and its consequence is a doubling. Two features of the sentence carry the weight. It is conditional throughout, so nothing is being reported, and the classical commentators say so explicitly. And the reason is not supplied here but drawn from the ayat around it: this household stands where everything it does is watched and copied. The doubling is presented as a function of position rather than as a stricter standard of character.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the sequence addressed to the household after the choice offered a few ayat earlier. The commentators treat these lines as setting out what the standing they had accepted actually involved. They emphasise the conditional form in their discussions, and note that the passage states a principle attached to a position rather than reporting anything that had occurred or was expected to.

keyTerms.note: A word for something excessive and openly ugly, used in the Quran of serious wrongs rather than of small faults. Its indefinite form keeps the whole sentence hypothetical rather than pointed.
An active participle, so the thing is described as making itself plain rather than as being proved by someone else. Attached to the noun it narrows the condition to what would be beyond dispute.
A dual from the word for a multiple. The same word appears once more in this surah, near its close, spoken by people asking that others be given double what they receive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leading household in a city that size lived without privacy. Its courtyard was a thoroughfare, delegations arrived and waited, and what happened inside was known across the settlement by evening. Standing carried that exposure everywhere in Arabia: a chief's family was watched closely because its conduct was read as the measure of his claim. This passage speaks inside that entirely public arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a doubling used here occurs twice in this surah and nowhere else in it. The second occurrence, near the surah's close, is spoken by people in the Fire asking that those who misled them be given double. So the same measure appears once as a burden attached to standing, and once as a request made in blame.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Weight of consequence is tied to position rather than to a person's worth, which is not the arrangement most readers assume. It implies that nearness to a source of guidance is a load as well as an honour. The following ayah completes the picture by doubling the reward on identical reasoning, and neither half works alone: a doubled risk without a doubled return would be a penalty rather than a station.

crossReferences.why: Completes the principle by doubling the reward on exactly the same reasoning.
Supplies the premise this ayah rests on, that the household is not situated like any other.
Describes a community made a witness over people, with the exposure that position carries.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place where you are watched more than you would like: at work, by a younger sibling, by your own children. This ayah treats that exposure as a real weight rather than as a compliment. Name one thing you do differently because of it, and decide today whether that difference is a burden you accept or a performance you have drifted into.

studies.title: A Reward Given Twice Over
studies.meaning: The counterpart to the previous ayah, and it is deliberately unequal to it. What draws the doubled reward is not simply the absence of the fault just named but three positive things: sustained devotion to God, the same towards His Messenger, and acting rightly. Then the reward is given twice, and a further provision is added beyond it and called generous. The commentators notice the asymmetry: one item was named on the other side, and three are asked for here.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, paired with the preceding ayah in the sequence addressed to the household of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The commentators read the two together as one arrangement with two faces and note that this half is the longer, adding a provision for which the warning has no counterpart at all. Nothing in the classical reports attaches either ayah to a particular incident.

keyTerms.note: A verb whose root joins continuous obedience to standing at length in prayer. It names a posture held over time rather than a series of separate acts, which is why it can carry a whole life's reward.

A dual of the word for an occasion or a turn, so the reward is counted in instances rather than weighed in amount. Set against the doubling in the previous ayah it makes the two sides answer each other.
An adjective used both of a person's character and of a thing's quality. Applied to provision it means plentiful and dignified at once, the kind of giving that does not shame whoever receives it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reward in that economy was normally proportional and negotiated. A guide, a guard, a share in a caravan's return: everything had a customary rate that people could and did argue about. Doubling belonged to the language of exceptional favour, the kind a patron extended once and everyone remembered for a generation. The ayah borrows that vocabulary and then adds something outside it entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for sustained devotion occurs about a dozen times in the Quran, and this surah holds two of them: this ayah, and the long list a few lines later where devoted men and devoted women are named side by side. The same word ties the household's description directly into the description of the whole community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is made to outrun consequence. The warning before this named one thing; this ayah names three, then pays twice and adds more on top, which leaves the two sides of the arrangement out of balance in one direction. That imbalance is the theological content of the pair. Position raises what is at stake on both sides, and the Quran's account of how it raises them is not symmetrical.

crossReferences.why: States the other half, where the same position doubles the weight of a fault.
Names devoted men and devoted women among the qualities rewarded across the whole community.
Says a group will be given their reward twice over, because of what they endured.

studies.applyIt: Notice which half of this pair you remember an hour from now. Most people carry the warning and forget the reward, though the reward is the longer sentence and the more generous arithmetic. Read the two ayat again in the other order tonight, reward first, and see whether the pairing feels different when you meet it that way round.

studies.title: Speak In A Known Way
studies.meaning: The ayah distinguishes this household from others and then immediately attaches a condition to the distinction: if you are mindful of God. What follows concerns a manner of speaking rather than the fact of it, since the closing clause requires speech and specifies only its register. The commentators read the middle clause as a matter of tone. The reason given is unusual, since the ayah names a disorder in a particular hearer rather than attributing anything to the speaker.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the sequence addressed to the household. The Prophet's house adjoined the place of prayer and people arrived at it constantly with questions, requests and disputes, so speech across a doorway was a daily occurrence rather than an exception. The commentators describe the instruction in exactly that setting: a public household in which conversation with visitors was routine and could not be avoided.
