Consequence, duration and isolation are stated first, and only then is a human voice allowed in, which means the regret is presented as a response to a settled situation rather than as a cause of anything. The wish also names obedience rather than belief, which locates the failure in what was done about what was already known.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about finding neither protector nor helper, in the middle of the siege.
Gives another wish of the same form, spoken by someone who took the wrong companion.
Puts a similar wish in a single line, after remembrance arrives too late to help.

studies.applyIt: Think of one piece of advice you have received more than twice from someone who was not trying to win an argument. You already know what it is. This passage is about the gap between hearing and doing, not between doubting and believing. Take the smallest possible step on that advice today, and notice how small the step actually was.

studies.title: We Obeyed Our Chiefs
studies.meaning: A second speech follows the first, and it is not a wish this time but an explanation. Two words are used for those who were followed, one for men of rank and one for men of consequence, and the pair occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Then a request is made, that the punishment of those leaders be doubled. The commentators observe what the speech does not contain: no claim to have been forced, and no denial of having obeyed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's closing sequence. The surah has described a community under pressure in which some people took their direction from figures whose commitment lay elsewhere, and it named the quiet persuasion that ran through households during the siege. These ayat give the eventual accounting for that following, spoken by the followers rather than by anyone else.

keyTerms.note: A plural for those at the head of a group, from a root for eminence and precedence. It names authority held by position, the kind a person is born into or acknowledged as holding.
A plural from the adjective for large, so it names those made big by standing rather than by office. Together with the previous word it covers both formal rank and mere prominence.
The causative of the verb for going astray, so it means they caused a losing of the way. Its object is the followers, but the verb reports what happened rather than removing anyone's part in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Following was the ordinary shape of Arabian life, not a failing. A man belonged to a clan, the clan had a head, and the head's judgement in a dispute or a treaty bound everyone under him. Standing apart from that meant losing protection, trade and marriage prospects at once. What the speech in this ayah describes was, at the time it happened, simply how a person lived in a tribe.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words used here for those who were followed appear together only in this one place in the Quran, and in these exact plural forms neither of them occurs anywhere else in the Book. The classical commentators explain the pairing as covering two distinct kinds of authority, formal position and sheer prominence, so that no version of being led escapes the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech is accurate and does not work. Everything in it is true: there were leaders, they were obeyed, and the way was lost. What it never states is that the following was compelled, and the passage lets the omission stand rather than answering it. Responsibility here is not divided between leader and follower so much as doubled, since the request for double punishment is granted its logic without relieving the speakers.

crossReferences.why: Stages the same exchange from the other side, with the followed answering the followers.
Extends the same dispute at length and has each side turn the argument back.
Describes the followed disowning those who followed them, and the wish for a return.

studies.applyIt: Name one person whose judgement you have quietly adopted without ever examining it, in politics, in work, in how you raise children. Not a bad person. Just someone whose conclusions you have been carrying as your own. Take one of those conclusions this week and work out whether you actually hold it. Most people have never once checked.

studies.title: Speak In A Straight Manner
studies.meaning: A warning drawn from an earlier community, then an instruction about speech. The believers are told not to be like those who caused hurt to Moses by what they said, and the text adds that God cleared him of it. The commentators record several accounts of what was said and do not settle on one, though they agree the injury was verbal and that it came from his own people. The instruction that follows names the alternative in a single word, used of an arrow that flies true and a wall built without a lean.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the end of a surah that has been dealing throughout with talk inside the community: rumour touching the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)'s household, the excuses of those who withdrew during the siege, and speech that damaged people who had done nothing. These two ayat generalise from the specific incidents the surah has been addressing into a standard for speech that outlasts the occasions which produced it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for injury that stops short of physical harm: annoyance, insult, the wearing damage of being talked about. It is the word the Quran uses for what words do rather than what hands do.
From the word for a face. Someone of standing is one whose face is known and welcomed, so the vindication is described in exactly the currency that the slander had attacked.
Used of an arrow that flies true and of a wall built without a lean. It names accuracy and soundness together, so right speech is defined by hitting the mark rather than by being pleasant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was the whole of a person's social capital, and it travelled by mouth through a town small enough for a story to cross it before noon. Satire was a recognised craft with paid practitioners, and a well-made line about a man could outlive him and follow his children. Nothing was written down to check a claim against, so a correction never travelled as fast as the original did.
studies.didYouKnow: Moses is named more often in the Quran than any other individual, well over a hundred times. Here he appears in none of the roles the name usually carries. He is not confronting Pharaoh, not receiving the tablets, not parting the sea. He is a man who was talked about unfairly by the people he had led, and who was cleared by someone other than himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The vindication is placed in God's hands: the text says God cleared him, not that he cleared himself. That has a consequence for anyone being spoken about, since it removes the obligation to win the argument. The instruction then turns to the other side of the exchange, the people doing the speaking, and the word it uses for right speech names accuracy and structural soundness rather than tact.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same territory in detail: ridicule, nicknames, suspicion, and speaking about people behind them.
Records Moses asking his own people directly why they injure him when they know who sent him.
Describes a rumour moving through a community and the sentence that should have stopped it.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last thing you passed on about someone that you had no way of checking. You do not need to undo it. Just let the next one stop with you: hear it, say nothing, and do not repeat it to the one person you would normally tell. Notice how strong the pull to pass it on actually is.

studies.title: He Will Set Your Deeds Right
studies.meaning: A promised result is attached to the instruction in the line before, and it arrives in two parts whose order repays attention. Conduct is repaired first, and only then are wrongs forgiven. Then a wider clause reaches past speech to obedience in general and names the outcome with a word meaning both escape and prize. The commentators read the causal link as the passage's real claim: one specific habit is adjusted, and the rest of a person's conduct follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the close of a surah that has spent much of its length on what people said. Rumours circulated during a siege, excuses were offered, sharp words followed once the danger lifted, and an accusation was made against innocent people. This ayah gives the promised result of the correction issued immediately before it. Commentators report no particular occasion and read the pair as the surah's practical summary.

keyTerms.note: A verb for mending what is broken and for making peace between people. Applied to deeds it implies they already exist and need adjusting, rather than that they must be started over.
A plural from a root for a tail, so the underlying image is of what trails along behind. It names consequences that follow a person rather than acts considered on their own.
A verb that carries both coming out safe and winning a prize. Both senses stay live in the Quran's usage, so the ayah ends on escape and gain in one word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's word was his working instrument. Contracts were oral, credit rested entirely on reputation, and a share in a caravan was settled by a handshake in front of witnesses who would be asked about it later. Straight speech was not only a virtue in that economy but the mechanism by which anything at all got done. The connection this ayah draws was visible in daily practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this ayah ends on, a great winning, occurs three times in the Quran, and all three are in Medinan surahs. In each of the three it stands at the very end of its ayah, functioning as a summing-up rather than as a description of anything in particular. The classical commentators treat it as a closing term of that kind.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness comes second, after repair, which reverses the order most readers expect and changes what is on offer. A wrong is not simply cancelled; the conduct that produced it is adjusted first. Treating speech as the lever is also a claim about how character actually changes. Not by resolving to become a different person, but by altering one observable habit and letting the rest come along behind it.

crossReferences.why: Gives in one clause the instruction whose result this ayah then promises.
Uses the same word for straight speech, about how the guardians of orphans should talk.
Ends with the same phrase for a great winning, after a promise of forgiveness.

studies.applyIt: Run the experiment this ayah describes. For one week, say only what you actually mean about small things: whether you are free, whether you liked it, whether you will be on time. Take on nothing larger than that. Then look at your conduct at the end of the week. The passage claims the one change pulls the other along.

studies.title: The Trust Nobody Else Took
studies.meaning: An offer is made to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they decline. The verb used is not refusal out of defiance but apprehension: they saw what it involved. Then a human being takes it up. The two words that close the ayah are intensive forms, and the commentators split over their tone. Some read them as an indictment of the recklessness in accepting; others as the explanation of why only a creature capable of failing could carry something that has to be freely kept. Both readings are recorded.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the close of a surah that has dealt throughout with people who kept their word and people who did not: those who held the ditch, those who found reasons to leave, those who spread rumour about a household. Placing this ayah at the end generalises the whole surah into one image. The commentators report no specific occasion for it and read it as a statement about the human condition.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for goods left in someone's keeping. It comes from the root meaning safety, the same root that gives the word for faith, so trustworthiness and belief share an origin.
A fear mixed with care rather than with cowardice, used of someone anxious about a responsibility they might mishandle. It describes weighing a burden accurately, not shrinking from it.
An intensive form. It names a disposition rather than an act, and paired with a matching form for ignorance it describes the standing tendencies of the creature that agreed to carry the deposit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deposits were everyday practice and there was no court to enforce them. A traveller leaving on a season-long journey left money, goods or documents with someone in the city and collected them on return, and the whole arrangement rested on the keeper's reputation. Mecca's trade could not have run otherwise. A man known to have returned what was left with him could borrow anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the trust in this ayah and the word for faith come from the same root, whose basic sense is safety and freedom from fear. In Arabic, being trustworthy and being a believer are built out of the same three letters, which is why the classical discussions of this ayah move between the two ideas without changing vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Human distinctiveness is located in a liability rather than in a capacity. What separates a person from a mountain here is not intelligence but the fact that something can be handed to them and lost. The two closing words then keep the account from becoming flattery: the creature that accepted is described in the same breath as prone to wrong and to ignorance, so the dignity and the risk are stated together.

crossReferences.why: Shows the angels raising the same objection in advance, given what they expect of the one being appointed.
Brings the word down to daily practice, deposits returned to the people they belong to.
Describes the original acknowledgement taken from the descendants of Adam, which the trust is often read alongside.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing currently sitting in your keeping that belongs to someone else: a message not answered, a tool borrowed, a task handed to you that has gone quiet. Deal with it this week. The ayah is about a deposit accepted, and deposits are lost by drift far more often than by decision.

studies.title: And He Turns To The Believers
studies.meaning: The last ayah of the surah is a purpose clause hanging off the one before it, and it works by an imbalance. Two groups are named for punishment and one for God's turning towards them, and only the second half arrives with no condition attached to it. The commentators observe where the surah has ended up: it opened by telling a man to accommodate nobody, and it closes on two names describing forgiveness and mercy as settled qualities.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the surah's final line. It follows the ayah in which a trust is offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains and taken up instead by the human being. The commentators read this ayah as giving the outcome of that acceptance, so the two halves of this sentence describe what becomes of a trust once somebody is actually carrying it. No separate occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A purpose particle fused to the verb, tying this ayah grammatically to the one before it. The whole sentence is a consequence clause and cannot be read standing on its own.
The verb of turning, with God as its subject and the believers as those turned towards. It is the same word used of a person repenting, and only the direction changes its sense.
An intensive form describing forgiveness as a settled attribute rather than an occasional act. It is the word the surah closes on, after seventy-two ayat of siege, failure and correction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The people who first heard this line had lived through everything the surah describes. They had dug a trench and held it through cold weeks on short rations, watched neighbours ask to withdraw, and heard what was said once the danger passed. A closing sentence naming forgiveness landed on an audience who could each identify exactly which of their own weeks it was covering.
studies.didYouKnow: Every pairing in this closing ayah names men and women separately, and the surah does the same thing at length some forty ayat earlier, in a list of ten qualities each given in both forms. That list is the most sustained example of the pattern anywhere in the Quran, and the final line repeats its shape, so the pairing frames the whole closing movement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah ends with mercy as the unconditional half of its last sentence. Punishment is named for those who set themselves against, and turning is named for the believers with nothing qualifying it, which is the reverse of where a reader expects to arrive after seventy-two ayat of exposure and correction. The two names at the very end describe a character rather than an act, so the surah's last word is about who God is.

crossReferences.why: Gives the trust this ayah is the consequence of, refused by everything else before a human took it.
Also pairs a turning towards the believers with those who would have them swerve away.
Describes God turning towards those who had wavered, including three who were left waiting.

studies.applyIt: Read this last line once with the whole surah behind you: a siege, a household, failures named one at a time, a hard passage near the end. Then notice which half of the sentence carries no condition. Most people would have written it the other way round. Sit with that for a minute before you close the page.
